evidence.claim: The Death Valley Scenic Byway follows two-lane SR 190 through the national park, crossing Panamint Valley and Towne Pass before dropping into Death Valley.
evidence.quote: The highway crosses the valley and then turns northeast over Towne Pass and into the northern part of Death Valley at Stovepipe Wells.

evidence.claim: two-lane SR 190 through the national park
evidence.quote: The route east of State Route 136 near Keeler is on the California Freeway and Expressway System, but is a two-lane road;

evidence.claim: The Federal Highway Administration describes sculpted hills, sand dunes and a route that dips below sea level.
evidence.quote: this byway travels through sculpted hills and shifting sand dunes and even dips below sea level.

evidence.claim: Its archived National Scenic Byway listing gives 81.5 miles and allows two hours to drive, or four hours to enjoy the route.
evidence.quote: National Scenic Byway • California Length 81.5 mi / 131.2 km Time to Allow Two hours to drive or four hours to enjoy the entire byway

evidence.claim: Towne Pass stands about 4,950 feet above sea level; Stovepipe Wells, below it to the east, stands less than ten feet above sea level.
evidence.quote: West on SR 190 is Towne Pass at about 4,950 feet (1,510 m) above sea level.

evidence.claim: Stovepipe Wells, below it to the east, stands less than ten feet above sea level.
evidence.quote: along State Route 190 (SR 190) at less than 10 feet (3.0 m) above sea level.

evidence.claim: Herman Eichbaum tried several approaches to securing a toll road before narrowing his plan to a connection between the area southeast of Darwin and his Stovepipe Wells resort.
evidence.quote: After several failures in getting a toll road approved from Lida, Nevada or over Towne Pass, he scaled back plans to include only the part of the latter route between southeast of Darwin and his resort at Stovepipe Wells.

evidence.claim: The road was certified complete in May 1926, with tolls of $2 per vehicle and 50 cents per person.
evidence.quote: The new Eichbaum Toll Road was certified complete on May 4, 1926, and toll rates were set: $2 per motor vehicle and 50¢ per person.

evidence.claim: The state bought it in 1934.
evidence.quote: in December 1934 the Division of Highways paid $25,000 for the 30.35-mile (48.84 km) road

evidence.claim: State and National Park Service paving followed, completed in 1937 with a cutoff that bypassed Darwin and the old toll road west of Panamint Springs.
evidence.quote: The work was completed in October 1937, including the 17.5-mile (18 km) Darwin cutoff that bypassed Darwin and the old toll road west of Panamint Springs.

evidence.claim: State and National Park Service paving followed
evidence.quote: The state Division of Highways and National Park Service soon paved the route

evidence.claim: From the western park entrance, the highway curves down into Panamint Valley, then crosses Towne Pass to Stovepipe Wells.
evidence.quote: After passing the turnoff to Darwin, SR 190 enters Death Valley National Park and becomes curvier as it heads down into the Panamint Valley. The highway crosses the valley and then turns northeast over Towne Pass and into the northern part of Death Valley at Stovepipe Wells.

evidence.claim: Continue southeast through the valley to Furnace Creek and the Badwater Basin turnoff.
evidence.quote: SR 190 turns southeast through Death Valley, which it remains inside until the turnoff to Badwater Basin, the lowest point in North America, near the settlement of Furnace Creek.

evidence.claim: The road climbs out beside Furnace Creek Wash, then turns east at the Dante's View turnoff toward the eastern park boundary.
evidence.quote: It leaves the valley to the southeast alongside Furnace Creek Wash, where the highway is usually closed at least once a year by flash floods. SR 190 turns east away from the wash at the turnoff to Dante's View, and soon leaves the park

evidence.claim: A length of stovepipe marked a waterhole when sand obscured it, giving Stovepipe Wells its name.
evidence.quote: When sand obscured the spot, a length of stovepipe was inserted as a marker; hence, its unique name.

evidence.claim: The historical marker also places the waterhole at the junction of two Indigenous trails.
evidence.quote: This waterhole, the only one in the sand dune area of Death Valley, was at the junction of the two Indian trails.

evidence.claim: During the mining booms at Rhyolite and Skidoo, this was the only known water source on the Cross-Valley road.
evidence.quote: During the bonanza days of Rhyolite and Skidoo, it was the only known water source on the Cross-Valley road.

evidence.claim: A temporary settlement began in 1906 as work started on a road between those towns.
evidence.quote: The first temporary settlement at Stovepipe Wells came into being when a road between Rhyolite and Skidoo was begun in 1906

evidence.claim: Tents offered travelers food, drink and lodging.
evidence.quote: A collection of tents was erected to serve travelers with food, drink and lodging.

evidence.claim: The namesake well lies northeast of the modern village.
evidence.quote: Stovepipe Well, for which the community is named, is shown to the northeast

evidence.claim: The village itself stands less than ten feet above sea level along SR 190.
evidence.quote: along State Route 190 (SR 190) at less than 10 feet (3.0 m) above sea level.

evidence.claim: The monument at Burnt Wagons records a decision to abandon the vehicles that had brought gold seekers into Death Valley.
evidence.quote: The name recalls the emigrants of 1849 who abandoned and burnt their wagons at the site.

evidence.claim: Its plaque identifies the Jayhawker group of Death Valley Forty-Niners, who entered the valley in 1849 seeking a shorter route to central California's mines.
evidence.quote: the Jayhawker group of Death Valley Forty-Niners, gold seekers from Middle West, who entered Death Valley in 1849 seeking short route to the mines of central California

evidence.claim: They burned their wagons, dried meat from some oxen, and continued west on foot with the surviving animals.
evidence.quote: burned their wagons, dried the meat of some oxen and, with surviving animals, struggled westward on foot.

evidence.claim: The former settlement near Stovepipe Wells is registered as California Historical Landmark 441.
evidence.quote: The site is now registered as California Historical Landmark #441.

evidence.claim: The former settlement near Stovepipe Wells
evidence.quote: Burnt Wagons is a former settlement in Inyo County, California, near Stovepipe Wells.

evidence.claim: Springs in the Amargosa Range created the natural oasis here.
evidence.quote: Springs in the Amargosa Range created a natural oasis at Furnace Creek

evidence.claim: Green alfalfa fields gave Greenland Ranch its first name in 1883.
evidence.quote: established Greenland Ranch in 1883, named after the green alfalfa fields which they planted there.

evidence.claim: A weather station followed in 1891, and the ranch became Furnace Creek Ranch in 1933.
evidence.quote: They established a weather station at the ranch in 1891. Greenland Ranch was renamed Furnace Creek Ranch in 1933.

evidence.claim: The weather station recorded 134°F on July 10, 1913, a measurement whose accuracy some meteorologists dispute.
evidence.quote: Furnace Creek holds the record for the highest recorded temperature in the world, reaching 134 °F (56.7 °C) on July 10, 1913. Some meteorologists dispute the accuracy of this measurement.

evidence.claim: The village stands 190 feet below sea level and houses the national park visitor center, museum and headquarters.
evidence.quote: The elevation of the village is 190 feet (58 m) below sea level. The visitor center, museum, and headquarters of Death Valley National Park are located at Furnace Creek.

evidence.claim: At the visitor center on SR 190, exhibits and a film cover the geology, climate, wildlife and human history of the park.
evidence.quote: Furnace Creek Visitor Center is located on CA-190 and includes exhibits and a film about the park's geology, climate, wildlife and natural history, as well as human history and pioneer experience.
